24	## 2. C2 auto-vectorization (SuperWord)
25	
26	- **What it vectorizes.** It applies SLP to innermost loop bodies after unrolling, and only to bodies with no control flow [S1]. Addresses must be linear in the loop counter, over arrays or (since JDK 26) MemorySegments [S2]. `Math.fma` loops compile to `vfmadd231ps` [S3]. Java may not fuse `a*b+c` [S4], and floating point has been strict everywhere since JDK 17 [S5]. No fast-math switch exists [I].
27	- **Float reductions (a dot product).**
28	  - JDK 9 vectorized reductions, with float/double add/mul reduced lane by lane in order; "simple" reductions were then disabled after regressions [S6].
29	  - JDK 21 (JDK-8302652) moved the reduction after the loop into a vector accumulator, only for reorderable operations (int/long, min/max) [S6].
30	  - JDK 26's cost model (JDK-8340093, merged 2025-11-10) vectorizes simple reductions when profitable [S6, S7], but "for float and double we cannot make add and mul faster than the scalar performance, because we cannot reorder the reduction" [S6].
31	  - On NEON (Apple Silicon included), strict-order float/double add/mul reductions are not auto-vectorized at all [S7, S8, S9]. A PR adding sequential NEON versions (JDK-8370677), open since 2026-05-07, reports 13–24% gains at n=256 and about 1% at n=4096 [S8].
32	  - So a scalar float dot product stays scalar in effect on JDK 25–27; the Vector API or hand-written accumulators are the way out [I].
33	- **Aliasing.** A loop whose load and store use different invariant offsets (`c[ci+j] += a*b[bi+j]`, c possibly b) needs a no-alias proof. JDK 26 adds speculative runtime alias checks with a multiversioned scalar fallback (JDK-8324751, integrated 2025-08-28) [S2, S10]. In 2017 C2 "choked on the array offsets" of a flat i-k-j matmul and emitted scalar code [S3].
34	- **Short loops.** Loops around 10 bytes regress slightly [S2], and JDK-8307084 (the vectorized drain loop is skipped for some small trip counts) was still in review in January 2026 [S11, not opened]. A 16-float row is short for C2 [I].

38	## 3. Half and reduced precision
39	
40	- `Float.floatToFloat16`/`float16ToFloat` are in `java.base` since JDK 20 [S1]; the value-based binary16 class `jdk.incubator.vector.Float16` since JDK 24 [S2]. JDK 25 auto-vectorizes Float16 arithmetic on x64 [§1-1]; `Float16Vector` arrives in JDK 28 [§1-7, I].
41	- A Lucene trial of a pre-integration `Float16Vector` build ran about 40× slower than float32 (2026-01-15) [S3]; re-measure [I].
42	- **bfloat16.** No JDK type; a `Bfloat16` "for testing purposes" lives only on Valhalla branches (2026-01) [S4, not opened]. On the JVM it means `short` storage and bit conversion with round-to-nearest-even [I].
43	- **Mixed precision.** The standard recipe keeps an fp32 master copy of the weights, scales the loss so small fp16 gradients survive, and accumulates fp16 products in fp32 [S5]. bf16 keeps fp32's exponent range and matched fp32 results without hyperparameter changes [S6].
44	- **For this model.** About 4K parameters (16 KB of float) sit in L1, so half precision saves bandwidth that is not the bottleneck. `float` in place of `double` is the step that pays: twice the lanes [I].

48	## 4. Project Valhalla
49	
50	- **JEP 401**, now "Value Objects (Preview)": Integrated, Release 28, page updated 2026-08-07 [S1]; JDK 28 GA is scheduled for 2027-03-09 [§1-5]. JEP 401 and JEP 539 are integrated, with EA builds at jdk.java.net/28 [S2]. It needs `--enable-preview`, under which the wrappers and `LocalDate` become value classes [S1].
51	- **Flattening.** The JVM may flatten references in fields and array elements, and scalarize them in locals, arguments and returns. Both are optimizations at the JVM's discretion [S1]. A flattened reference must be read and written atomically, which "on common hardware" limits mutable fields (and array elements) to 64 bits including a null flag. Fields of value classes are exempt [S1]. An array of a value class holding two floats (64 bits plus the null flag) or two doubles is therefore not flattened in JDK 28 [I from S1]. Scalarization has no size limit [S1].
52	- **Null-restricted types.** The draft JEP "Null-Restricted Value Class Types" adds null-free storage and an opt-in to non-atomic flat arrays (`LooselyConsistentValue`). It is still a draft (updated 2026-05-28) with no target [S3]. Nullness markers are a separate draft (updated 2025-07-24) [S4].
53	- **Generic specialization.** "Parametric JVM" is one of five planned feature sets, with no JEP [S2].
54	- **Vector API.** The plan is to declare vector classes as value classes (the lworld+vector branch) and to use generic specialization, after which `IntVector`-style subclasses "might not be required" [§1-3].
55	- **How long in preview.** A secondary article (2026-11-10) reports that the language architect called a JDK 29 exit from preview "optimistic" [S5, not verified].

76	## 6. Parallelism for small dense work
77	
78	- **ForkJoinTask.** "As a very rough rule of thumb, a task should perform more than 100 and less than 10000 basic computational steps"; tasks that are too small let overhead "overwhelm processing" [S1].
79	- **Parallel streams.** They pay only when the sequential version takes more than "roughly (within a factor of ten of) 100 microseconds", that is N×Q ≥ 10000. Misuse "might cost you around 100 microseconds", partly from waking idle cores [S2].
80	- **Virtual threads** "are not faster threads … They exist to provide scale (higher throughput), not speed (lower latency)". More threads than cores does not help CPU-bound work [S3].
81	- **For this model.** A whole step is about 100 µs, the threshold itself; one 16×16 matmul (about 4K FMAs) is two or three orders below it, so splitting inside a matmul loses [I from S1, S2]. Split across examples: one long-lived thread per core, each with a batch slice above 100 µs, a barrier, then one fixed-order gradient reduction [I]. The llama2.java data (§5) fits this.

85	## 7. GEMM on the CPU without BLAS
86	
87	- **The method.** Layer loops for the caches, pack panels so the inner kernel streams from L1/L2, hold a block of C in registers [S1]; thread the outer loops around a small micro-kernel [S2]; for small shapes, JIT one kernel per shape [S3].
88	- **At 16×16 to 64×16.** Each float matrix is at most 4 KB, so all operands sit in L1 and packing and cache blocking are moot. What matters is register tiling (several C row-vectors held in registers, a broadcast A[i,k], fma with B row-vectors), full unrolling for the fixed shapes, and a layout per pass that avoids transposes (forward X·W; backward dX = dY·Wᵀ, dW = Xᵀ·dY) [I from S1, S3].
89	- **Java against peak.**
90	  - 2017–18, Skylake (32 SP flops/cycle per core): Java i-k-j with `Math.fma` on JDK 10 barely passed 4 flops/cycle; GCC auto-vectorized C held about 7; hand-written AVX2 intrinsics reached about 23–26 (about 80%) [S4, S5].
91	  - The Vector API dgemm reached 60% of OpenBLAS (2021) [§1-12].
92	  - Tiled Vector API: 23 GFLOP/s on one AVX2 core [§1-13], which I put at roughly 20–30% of peak [I].
93	  - For reference, an M1 P-core's NEON peak is 102.4 GFLOP/s fp32 and 51.2 fp64, estimated at 3.2 GHz [S6].
94	  - I found no Java measurement at 16–64 sizes [I].

98	## 8. Relaxed reduction order in training
99	
100	- **Java.** Scalar floating point is strictly ordered, so a JVM never reorders a sum; the program or code generator has to (multiple accumulators, Vector API, a tree) [§2, I]. The JDK already relaxes order where an API allows it. `DoubleStream.sum` leaves its order "intentionally not defined", may use compensated summation, and its "output … may vary on the same input elements" [S1]. Likewise `reduceLanes` [§1-17].
101	- **Error bounds.** Worst case grows as O(εn) for recursive summation, O(ε log n) for pairwise, and O(ε) independent of n for Kahan, at several times the arithmetic. NumPy and Julia sum pairwise by default [S2, after Higham 1993].
102	- **What frameworks guarantee.**
103	  - PyTorch: no reproducibility across releases, platforms or CPU and GPU; `use_deterministic_algorithms` makes nondeterministic operations raise [S3].
104	  - cuBLAS: bitwise reproducible run to run "on GPUs with the same architecture and the same number of SMs", barring multi-stream and atomics modes; not across versions [S4].
105	  - LLM inference: the forward pass is "run-to-run deterministic"; variance comes from batch-size-dependent reduction order; atomics appear in FlashAttention backward; batch-invariant kernels cost about 20% [S5].
106	- **On a CPU,** a reduction tree fixed in shape (independent of thread count) gives bit-reproducible batches at almost no cost [I].

110	## 9. LMAX Disruptor, Agrona, FFM off-heap memory
111	
112	- **Disruptor** is "A High Performance Inter-Thread Messaging Library" (4.0.0 requires Java 11) [S1, S2]. It offers nothing for arithmetic. Its discipline still applies: preallocate, one writer per region, and pad per-thread gradient buffers against false sharing [I].
113	- **Agrona** has "buffers for working with on and off heap memory with memory ordering semantics", primitive collections, queues, ring buffers and agents [S3]. Its buffers go through a generated `UnsafeApi` over `jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe`, and its build opens `java.base/jdk.internal.misc` [S4]. That gives typed, byte-addressed access, not vector math [I].
114	- **Unsafe memory access** was deprecated for removal in JDK 23 (JEP 471) and warns by default from JDK 24 (JEP 498). Phase 3, deny by default, is planned "in JDK 26 or later" [S5, S6]. No JEP for it appears in the JDK 26 or 27 feature lists, nor in JDK 28's as of 2026-11-11 [§1-4, §1-5].
115	- **FFM** (`MemorySegment`, `Arena`) is final since JDK 22 [S7]. It gives off-heap memory, more than 2 GB, mmap (llama3.java uses it), explicit alignment and deterministic freeing [S7, §5-2].
116	- **Speed against arrays.** On AArch64 (2025-06), a Vector API dot product took 61 ns on arrays against 95–99 ns on segments, whose loop bound was not hoisted [S8]. A scalar add loop (2025-09-29) took 167 ns on arrays, 549 on segments and 600–777 with Unsafe on JDK 25; on JDK 26 arrays took 210, segments 136, Unsafe much as before. The JDK 26 gain is credited mainly to JDK-8324751 [S9, S10].
117	- **For this model,** one owned `float[]` block is simplest and fastest on JDK 25; segments become competitive on JDK 26+ [I].
118	
119	Sources: 1 https://github.com/LMAX-Exchange/disruptor (README) · 2 https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LMAX-Exchange/disruptor/master/src/docs/asciidoc/en/changelog.adoc · 3 https://github.com/aeron-io/agrona (README, © 2014–2025) · 4 Agrona `build.gradle` and `UnsafeBuffer.java` on master (2026-11-20) · 5 https://openjdk.org/jeps/471 (JDK 23) · 6 https://openjdk.org/jeps/498 (JDK 24) · 7 https://openjdk.org/jeps/454 (JDK 22; not opened) · 8 https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/panama-dev/2025-June/021066.html · 9 https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/panama-dev/2025-September/021142.html (2025-09-29) · 10 https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/panama-dev/2025-September/021143.html
120	
121	## 10. GraalVM and Truffle (briefly)
122	
123	- In September 2025 Oracle detached GraalVM from the Java release train to focus on non-Java languages; GraalVM for JDK 24 was the last "licensed and supported as part of Oracle Java SE Products" [S1].
124	- GraalVM 25.x (on JDK 25) continues: 25.2.4 (2026-07-28) turns Vector API support on by default in Native Image [S2]; 25.3.4.1 (2026-08-25) adds default-on loop vectorization for "eligible array-arithmetic loops" [S3]. llama3.java calls Graal 25+'s Vector API support "partial but good" [§5-2]; in 2023 it had none [§5-1].
125	- I found no 2026 Graal-against-C2 numeric benchmark. Truffle serves AST interpreters; a bytecode compiler gains nothing from it [I].
126	
127	Sources: 1 https://www.infoq.com/news/2025/09/java-news-roundup-sep15-2025 (2025-09-23) · 2 https://www.graalvm.org/release-notes/25.2/ (2026-07-28) · 3 https://www.graalvm.org/release-notes/25.3/ (2026-08-25)
128	
129	## 11. The handover's JVM claims
130	
131	**JVM tooling status**
132	
133	1. *"On JDK 25 … primitive arrays plus the incubating Vector API … value classes are not."* **Holds**; FFM is final too, but its loops vectorize poorly on JDK 25 (§9).
134	2. *Primitive arrays "flat, unboxed, not scanned by the GC".* **Holds**; copying collectors still move them [I].
135	3. *Vector API "tenth incubator in JDK 25 (JEP 508)".* **Holds**; twelfth in JDK 27, no API change since (§1).
136	4. *`--add-modules` at compile and run time; package renamed on leaving incubation.* **Both hold** (JEP 11); a module can `requires` it instead.
137	5. *FFM: "Final"; "supported replacement for Unsafe memory access".* **Holds.** *"Worth it only to hand memory to native BLAS".* **Wrong** in general: it is also how to mmap weights, pass 2 GB, align and free deterministically, and on JDK 26 its loops beat arrays in one benchmark (§9). For this model, `float[]` remains the choice on JDK 25.
138	6. *Value classes: "Preview in JDK 28, due March 2027; early-access builds exist"; not in JDK 25; needs `--enable-preview`.* **Holds**: JEP 401, retitled "Value Objects (Preview)", is Integrated for Release 28, GA 2027-03-09, EA builds exist (§4). *"Expected to stay in preview through JDK 29".* **Not verified** (one secondary source, §4-5).
139	7. *JEP 401 page stale, status unverified.* **Now verified**: Integrated, Release 28, updated 2026-08-07.
140	8. *"A vector is an ordinary heap object … speed depends on C2 proving it never escapes … otherwise each operation allocates".* **Holds in substance**: C2 uses vector-specific box elimination, not plain escape analysis; boxes appear where a vector escapes, and the Java fallback allocates (§1). The advice is right.
141	9. *"Why the Vector API waits for Valhalla".* **Holds** as the JEPs state it (incubate until Valhalla preview, then preview); they also name generic specialization as a reason the shape may change (§1-3).
142	10. *"Valhalla matters only if a value object (a dual number) should live flat inside an array".* **Partly wrong.** In JDK 28 a dual of two floats or two doubles exceeds the 64-bit atomic limit with its null flag, so its arrays stay unflattened until the null-restricted/non-atomic draft, which has no target (§4). Scalarization helps duals in locals, and Valhalla matters for the Vector API's own types.
143	
144	**Design direction**
145	
146	11. *"Threading inside one multiply will lose to scheduling overhead".* **Holds** (§6: about a 100 µs threshold; a 16×16 matmul is far below it).
147	12. *"Parallelism pays across examples … reduce per-example gradients".* **Holds** [I], provided each worker's slice exceeds about 100 µs and the reduction tree is fixed (§6, §8).
148	13. *"Strict IEEE ordering blocks SIMD" for the inner dot product.* **Holds** for C2; on NEON it does not vectorize float add reductions at all in JDK 25–27 (§2). *"Declaring `+` associative licenses multiple accumulators and vector lanes".* **Holds only at source level**: the JVM takes no such declaration, so the code generator must emit the reordered code (accumulators or Vector API).
149	14. *"i-k-j … elementwise and vectorises under strict IEEE".* **Holds in principle; conditional on JDK 25**: flat arrays with different invariant offsets may not vectorize before JDK 26's alias checks, 16-element rows are short loops for C2, and `a*b+c` is never fused (emit `Math.fma`) (§2). Measure, or write the kernel in the Vector API.
150	15. *"GPU kernels reduce nondeterministically and runs are not bit-reproducible".* **Partly.** Reproducibility is not guaranteed across platforms or releases, and atomics kernels are nondeterministic, but cuBLAS is bitwise reproducible run to run on one GPU type, forward passes are mostly deterministic, and deterministic modes exist (§8).
151	16. *"Relax associativity only; keep NaN and infinity".* **Consistent with the JVM**, which has no fast-math mode (§2, §8).
152	17. *"Keep long accumulations in higher precision".* **Holds**: the mixed-precision recipe (§3).
153	18. *"Prefer float … on 128-bit NEON it doubles the lane count".* **Holds**: 4 lanes against 2 (§1).
154	
155	From the "set aside" table: arrays beat `Unsafe` on JDK 25 **holds** (167 against 600–777 ns); Agrona as "byte-oriented buffers outside the GC heap" is **partly** right, since its buffers wrap heap or off-heap memory; Disruptor as "a messaging structure" **holds** (§9).

3:# The pure-Java microGPT: the baseline of P-7, and its timings
7:## 1. What was built
22:## 2. What it reproduces of the checks

195:## 6. Fork/join: the baseline in the shape of the library and the compiled runtime
288:## 7. The rehearsal's loop
302:## 8. The lines of the Fortress that were hardest to read as an algorithm
311:## 9. For the record

45	## 3. What could not be matched, and what was chosen
46	
47	**The order of the sums longer than 16 terms, and only that.** Everything else the Java computes by the operations of the Fortress source in its order: a division stays a division (no reciprocal), no fused multiply-add, the masked attention entries and the padded rows are computed as the Fortress computes them, `10.0^(-5)` is the folded constant `1e-5` and `beta1^t` is `Math.pow`, as walk's native is (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleDoubleArith.java:76-78`).
48	
49	- The library's matrix product adds the terms of each element in ascending order of the summed index: `Matrix.mul` splits the summed dimension in sequence, and forks only the rows and the columns (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3044-3102`). The Java's products add in the same order. Only the first term differs in form (the library stores it, the Java adds it to 0.0), which cannot change a value other than the sign of a zero.
50	- The library's `DOT`, `SUM` and `BIG MAX` are reductions over a range. A range of more than `grainSize` = 16 elements splits at a power-of-two boundary and joins the two results (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:20`, `:1310-1327`); at most 16 elements fold left to right from the identity (`:1365-1373`). In the model at batch 1 the only sums of more than 16 terms are the softmax over the 27 logits (`sm` on line 61), which the library adds as (16 terms) + (11 terms). The Java adds all 27 left to right. That is the last-digit difference from walk above. The fork/join variant of section 6 adds them as the library does.
51	- With more than one document in a batch, `SUM vm` and the loss's `DOT` are also longer than 16.
52	
53	**The parser is ported, not replaced.** `FlatData.parseFloat` accumulates the mantissa digit by digit in a double and scales once, so it is not correctly rounded. `./run.sh parse`:
54	
55	    4192 numbers, 699 differ from Double.parseDouble, the worst by 2.0 ulp
56	
57	So 699 of the 4,192 initial parameters that the flat program trains from are not the doubles nearest to the decimal text of the weight files. The Java uses the same arithmetic, so that it starts from the same parameters; with `Double.parseDouble` it would start from other ones. The loader check passes at tolerance 0 either way, because it reads `P0.txt` through the same parser.
58	
59	**Decisions.** No decision of the curator covers these; each says which reading was acted on.
60	
61	1. *Same operations per element, sums left to right.* The alternative, reordering sums or replacing divisions where the tolerance holds, would be faster in places (section 5) and was not taken in the baseline, so that a ratio of compiled Fortress to this program measures the implementation and not a different arithmetic. The Vector API variant shows what one reordering buys.
62	2. *Dense, as the Fortress.* All 16 positions of every document are computed, and all 16 by 16 attention entries, also those that the mask sends to exactly 0. Skipping them is an algorithmic saving open to both programs alike.
63	3. *Storage reused.* One step's arrays are allocated once per batch size and reused, and `adam` updates `p`, `m` and `v` in place, where the Fortress makes new arrays and returns three new vectors. What this saves was not measured.
64	4. *Products read the weights in place.* `x w^T` is a dot product of two rows. A version that copied each transposed weight matrix first, so that the inner loop ran along rows of both operands, measured the same within noise in one fork (step 109 against 101 microseconds, taken at different loads) and was dropped.
65	5. *No lambdas.* The row bodies are anonymous classes. With lambdas the first step of a cold JVM took 30 ms instead of 5 ms (one run each), the cost of the first lambda's bootstrap.
66	6. *The model reaches loops and sums through four seams* (`forRange`, `dot`, `sum`, `max` in `FlatArrays`), so that the two variants replace the vocabulary alone. After warm-up the step measured the same with and without the seams (101.9 against 100.9 and 102.5 microseconds, one or two forks each).
67	
68	## 4. Timings of the baseline
69	
70	### Method
71	
72	- Machine: 4 CPUs, Intel Xeon @ 2.30GHz (AVX-512), 15 GB, a cloud container shared with other sessions, which were building and running throughout. The load average is given with every run; it was never below 1.
73	- JDK: OpenJDK 25.0.4.1 (`/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64`, the JDK of `experiment/env.sh`), 64-bit server VM, mixed mode, class-data sharing on. Flags: none; `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` unset, as `env.sh` does. So: tiered compilation, G1, the default heap. The program has one thread; the JVM's compiler and collector threads run beside it on the other CPUs.

195	## 6. Fork/join: the baseline in the shape of the library and the compiled runtime
196	
197	`variants/forkjoin/FlatArrays.java` gives the vocabulary's loops and sums the shape that the Fortress library and its compiled runtime give parallel work, on a `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool`. What a piece computes once it is no longer split is the baseline's plain loop, so its time is a floor for what compiled Fortress could reach with this structure and unboxed arrays.
198	
199	| Shape | In the tree | In the variant |
200	|---|---|---|
201	| a parallel range | `Library/RangeInternals.fss:1310-1345`: a range of more than `grainSize` = 16 elements (`:20`) splits at the highest power-of-two boundary inside it; the two parts are the arms of a `do ... also do` | `forRange`, used by the model's row loops (`rows(rmsn)`, `rows(sm)`, ...), by `adam`'s loop over the 4,192 elements, by the loop over the planes and by the elementwise passes |
202	| a reduction | the same split, the two results joined; at most 16 elements fold left to right (`:1365-1373`) | `dot`, `sum`, `max`: no shared accumulator |
203	| the matrix product | `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3044-3102`: the largest of the three dimensions is halved by `partition` (the largest power of two below it); the halves of the rows and of the columns are forked, the halves of the summed dimension run in sequence; it stops at one element | `mma`, under `mul`, `mulT`, `addMulT`, `tMul` and on each plane under the three `heads*` |
204	| the arms | `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:1717-1770` and `runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java`: every arm but the first becomes a task object; `forkIfProfitable` forks it if the pool has more than one thread and the worker's surplus of queued tasks is at most the spawn threshold (5, `FortressExecutable.java:26`); the first arm runs in place; `joinOrRun` joins the task or runs it in place | `Arm`: the same two methods; the program's body runs as a task of the pool |

1	(* MicroGptFlat -- microGPT in native Fortress arrays, data designed after Hsu
     2	   (Run C4, the synthesis of rounds two and three: explorations/run-c4/design.md).
     3	   The model only: hyperparameters, the layout table, the four vector
     4	   functions, the step, Adam and the training loop, line for line against
     5	   explorations/apl/reference/hsu-flat/microgpt_concise.dyalog and the formulas
     6	   (the tour: explorations/run-c4/tour.md).  The array vocabulary is FlatArrays,
     7	   the loaders and the corpus FlatData.  Run from explorations/run-c4/src: the
     8	   paths are relative. *)
     9	component MicroGptFlat
    10	export MicroGptFlat
    11	export Executable
    12	import FlatArrays.{...}
    13	import FlatData.{...}
    14	import System.{...}
    15	
    16	(* --------------------------------------------------- hyperparameters ---- *)
    17	(nEmbd, blockSize, nHead, headDim, vocabSize, bosId) = (16, 16, 4, 4, 27, 26)
    18	(epsilon, lr0, beta1, beta2, epsilon_A, nSteps) = (10.0^(-5), 0.01, 0.85, 0.99, 10.0^(-8), 1000)
    19	(corpusPath, weightsDir) = ("../../apl/reference/dzaima/docs.txt", "../../apl/reference/dzaima/w")
    20	
    21	(* -------------------------------------- rmsn, sm and their backward ------ *)
    22	rmsn(x: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = x / SQRT (epsilon + (x DOT x) / |x|)
    23	sm(z: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = do e = exp(z - (BIG MAX z)); e / (∑ e) end
    24	mask: Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = mat(blockSize, blockSize, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 => if j > i then -(10.0^10) else 0.0 end)
    25	rmsn_b(dy: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], x: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = do
    26	    r = SQRT (epsilon + (x DOT x) / |x|); y = x / r
    27	    (dy - y ((y DOT dy) / |y|)) / r
    28	  end
    29	sm_b(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], dy: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = p × (dy - (p DOT dy))
    30	
    31	(* ------------------------------- tactic 2/8: one vector, nine views ------ *)
    32	matName(i: ZZ32): String =
    33	    if i = 0 then "wte" elif i = 1 then "wpe" elif i = 2 then "lm_head" elif i = 3 then "attn_wq" elif i = 4 then "attn_wk"
    34	    elif i = 5 then "attn_wv" elif i = 6 then "attn_wo" elif i = 7 then "mlp_fc1" else "mlp_fc2" end
    35	matShape(i: ZZ32): (ZZ32, ZZ32) =
    36	    if (i = 0) OR (i = 2) then (vocabSize, nEmbd) elif i = 7 then (4 nEmbd, nEmbd) elif i = 8 then (nEmbd, 4 nEmbd) else (nEmbd, nEmbd) end
    37	matCount(i: ZZ32): ZZ32 = do (r, c) = matShape(i); r c end
    38	matOffset(i: ZZ32): ZZ32 = ∑[j <- 0#i] matCount(j)
    39	nParams(): ZZ32 = matOffset(9)
    40	view(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], i: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do (r, c) = matShape(i); view(p, matOffset(i), r, c) end
    41	
    42	(* -------------------- tactic 3/5: the corpus as one padded integer matrix - *)
    43	corpus: Corpus = loadCorpus(corpusPath, blockSize, bosId)
    44	
    45	(* ------------------------- the step: keys -> (loss, flat gradient). Pure. -- *)
    46	step(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], b: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\]): (RR64, Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]) = do
    47	    ids = corpus.tokens(b, 0); tg = corpus.tokens(b, 1); vm = corpus.valid(b); nv = ∑ vm; pos = corpus.positions(b)
    48	    (wte, wpe, lm, wq, wk, wv, wo, f1, f2) = (view(p, 0), view(p, 1), view(p, 2), view(p, 3), view(p, 4), view(p, 5), view(p, 6), view(p, 7), view(p, 8))
    49	    h(m: Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = heads(m, blockSize, nHead, headDim)
    50	    u(t: Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = unheads(t, nHead)
    51	    (* -- forward, all (doc, pos) rows at once -- *)
    52	    x = gather(wte, ids) + gather(wpe, pos); xp = rows(rmsn, x); x1 = rows(rmsn, xp)
    53	    (q, k, v) = (x1 wq^T, x1 wk^T, x1 wv^T); (qh, kh, vh) = (h(q), h(k), h(v))
    54	    a = rows(sm, mask + (qh kh^T) / SQRT (1.0 headDim)); hc = u(a vh)
    55	    x2 = xp + hc wo^T; x3 = rows(rmsn, x2); m0 = x3 f1^T; mr = 0.0 MAX m0; x4 = x2 + mr f2^T
    56	    pr = rows(sm, x4 lm^T); loss = -(vm DOT log(pick(pr, tg))) / nv
    57	    (* -- backward, one line under each forward line, bottom-up -- *)
    58	    dL = diag(vm / nv) (pr - onehot(tg, vocabSize)); gLM = dL^T x4; dX4 = dL lm
    59	    gF2 = dX4^T mr; dM0 = (dX4 f2) × (m0 > 0.0); gF1 = dM0^T x3; dX3 = dM0 f1
    60	    dX2 = dX4 + rows(rmsn_b, dX3, x2); gWO = dX2^T hc; dh = h(dX2 wo)
    61	    dVh = a^T dh; dS = rows(sm_b, a, dh vh^T) / SQRT (1.0 headDim)
    62	    dQh = dS kh; dKh = dS^T qh; (dQ, dK, dV) = (u(dQh), u(dKh), u(dVh))
    63	    (gWQ, gWK, gWV) = (dQ^T x1, dK^T x1, dV^T x1); dX1 = dQ wq + dK wk + dV wv
    64	    dXp = dX2 + rows(rmsn_b, dX1, xp); dX = rows(rmsn_b, dXp, x)
    65	    gWTE = (onehot(ids, vocabSize))^T dX; gWPE = (onehot(pos, blockSize))^T dX
    66	    (loss, flat(gWTE, gWPE, gLM, gWQ, gWK, gWV, gWO, gF1, gF2))
    67	  end
    68	
    69	(* --------------------- Adam: three whole-vector expressions over p, m, v -- *)
    70	adam(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], m: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], v: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], g: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], t: ZZ32, lr: RR64):
    71	    (Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]) = do
    72	    m' = beta1 m + (1 - beta1) g
    73	    v' = beta2 v + (1 - beta2) (g × g)
    74	    p' = p - (lr (m' / (1 - beta1^t))) / (SQRT (v' / (1 - beta2^t)) + epsilon_A)
    75	    (p', m', v')
    76	  end
    77	learningRate(s: ZZ32): RR64 = lr0 (1 - (1.0 s) / nSteps)
    78	
    79	(* --------------------------------------------------- training ----------- *)
    80	run(): () = do
    81	    println "microgpt flat | params " nParams() " | corpus " corpus.size() " x " (blockSize + 1) " | batch 1, 5 steps"
    82	    bsz = 1
    83	    p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] := loadParams(weightsDir, matName, 9, nParams())
    84	    m: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] := zeros(nParams())
    85	    v: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] := zeros(nParams())
    86	    for s <- seq(0#5) do
    87	        t0 = nanoTime()
    88	        (l, g) = step(p, keys(bsz, fn (i: ZZ32): ZZ32 => (s bsz + i) MOD corpus.size()))
    89	        (p, m, v) := adam(p, m, v, g, s + 1, learningRate(s))
    90	        println "step " (s + 1) " loss " l "  (" ((nanoTime() - t0) DIV 1000000) " ms)"
    91	    end
    92	  end
    93	end

(* MicroGptFlatCheck -- the standard of success for Run C4 (round three's check
   with round two's four single-document checks added, 40 in all), one line per
   check with the measured difference and PASS or FAIL, against the goldens of
   Run C (explorations/run-c/goldens, extracted from
   explorations/experiment/run-c-goldens/goldens.json), then an aggregate verdict; any FAIL
   ends the run with a non-zero status.
   Run from explorations/run-c4/src:  ../../../bin/fortress MicroGptFlatCheck.fss *)
component MicroGptFlatCheck
export Executable
import MicroGptFlat.{...}
import FlatArrays.{...}
import FlatData.{...}
import System.{...}

goldensDir: String = "../../run-c/goldens"
tolLoss: RR64 = 10.0^(-12)
tolGrad: RR64 = 10.0^(-12)
tolFd: RR64 = 10.0^(-8)

passed: ZZ32 := 0
failed: ZZ32 := 0
report(name: String, diff: RR64, tol: RR64): () = do
    ok = diff <= tol
    if ok then passed += 1 else failed += 1 end
    println name ": diff " diff " " (if ok then "PASS" else "FAIL" end)
  end
maxAbsDiff(a: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], b: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): RR64 = BIG MAX[\RR64\][i <- 0#|a|] |a[i] - b[i]|

run(): () = do
    println "MicroGptFlat checks (Run C4) | threads " (getProperty("fortress.threads", "?")) " | tolerances: loss " tolLoss " grad " tolGrad " fd " tolFd
    wall0 = nanoTime()
    p0 = loadParams("../../apl/reference/dzaima/w", matName, 9, nParams())
    (* 0. the loaders against the goldens' P0 and corpus rows *)
    report("loader: max |P - P0| over 4192", maxAbsDiff(p0, readVector(goldensDir "/P0.txt", 4192)), 0.0)
    lines = readLines(goldensDir "/corpus_first16.txt")
    corpusDiff = BIG MAX[\RR64\][d <- 0#16] do
        nums = numbersOf(lines[d].beyond(' '))   (* the line is: name len t0 .. t16; nums[0] is len *)
        (BIG MAX[\RR64\][j <- 0#17] |nums[1 + j] - (1.0 corpus.token(d, j))|) MAX |nums[0] - (1.0 corpus.length(d))|
      end
    report("corpus: max |row - golden| over documents 0..15", corpusDiff, 0.0)

    scale(t1: T): Matrix[\T,s0,s1\] = cast[\Matrix[\T,s0,s1\]\](map[\T\](fn (e:T):T => t1 e))
    mul[\ nat s2 \](other: Matrix[\T,s1,s2\]): Matrix[\T,s0,s2\] = do
        res = matrix[\T,s0,s2\]()
        mma(a:ZZ32,i:ZZ32,b:ZZ32,j:ZZ32,c:ZZ32,k:ZZ32):() =
            if k>=i AND k>=j then
              if k=1 then
                pr : T = get(a,b) other.get(b,c)

                res.put((a,c), res.get(a,c) + pr)
              else
                (k0,k1) = partition(k)
                do
                  mma(a,i,b,j,c,k0)
                also do
                  mma(a,i,b,j,c+k0,k1)
                end
              end
            elif j>=i then
                (j0,j1) = partition(j)
                mma(a,i,b,j0,c,k)
                mma(a,i,b+j0,j1,c,k)
            else
                (i0,i1) = partition(i)
                do
                  mma(a,i0,b,j,c,k)
                also do
                  mma(a+i0,i1,b,j,c,k)
                end
            end
        mm(a:ZZ32,i:ZZ32,b:ZZ32,j:ZZ32,c:ZZ32,k:ZZ32):() =
            if k>=i AND k>=j then
              if k=1 then
                res.put((a,c), get(a,b) other.get(b,c))
              else
                (k0,k1) = partition(k)
                do
                  mm(a,i,b,j,c,k0)
                also do
                  mm(a,i,b,j,c+k0,k1)
                end
              end
            elif j>=i then
                (j0,j1) = partition(j)
                mm(a,i,b,j0,c,k)
                mma(a,i,b+j0,j1,c,k)
            else
                (i0,i1) = partition(i)
                do
                  mm(a,i0,b,j,c,k)
                also do
                  mm(a+i0,i1,b,j,c,k)
                end
            end
        if s0=0 OR s1=0 OR s2=0 then

        else
          mm(0,s0,0,s1,0,s2)
          res
        end
      end

POSITIONS.md:7
- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.** The revival judges what the designers intended by the team's own sources: its Working Draft of February 2011, its texts on types and its code. `Specification/` holds the Working Draft as a living document: the revival revises it and states each change (P-95). The texts on types include the Types chapter of the specification's 2012 restart (P-25). In `Papers/`, they include the OOPSLA 2011 paper, Naden's 2012 write-up and the POPL 2019 paper with its technical report. P-26 says when code counts, and which source wins where two conflict. The revival does not redesign the language. A pure-Java microGPT is the baseline that compiled microGPT is measured against: the optimal result, the one to aim at.

----
POSITIONS.md:16
- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.

----
POSITIONS.md:111
- P-84 **On the compiled path, the array of every number type is to be stored unboxed, in a Java array of its primitive type, and every array is to have the most efficient store that its element type allows; arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes in their types.** `RR64` goes in a `double[]`, `ZZ32` in an `int[]`, and so on, for each number type that has a Java primitive type; `RR64`'s `double[]`, the model's, is the first case. Why: a high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. So the storage and the sizes are one design: the sizes stay in the array types as `nat` static parameters, as the library's `Vector` and `Matrix` declare them, and the compiled checker checks them. The sizes do not wait while a first version of the store carries them only as run-time fields; that layered plan was rejected. Both halves follow the library's own patterns (P-27, on extending the library in its own way). The compiled checker checks `nat` static parameters (F-67). The class loader, as it makes a generic instance's class, only renames the type parameter, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field; a loader that would, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), is unmeasured (F-18).

----
POSITIONS.md:112
- P-85 **The array design's three questions are open, with no default, and return after the switch-over with the array decisions A, B and D.** The array design is the compiled path's design for arrays. The three questions: how the array factory chooses the store of each element type; whether the store also keeps the size as a field, beside the size in the type; and whether a factory for a size known only at run time returns the unsized `Array[\E,I\]`, whose type holds no size. These questions are apart from decisions A, B and D: decision A is how an array of a number type, made through the library's generic array traits, gets its unboxed store, `RR64`'s `double[]` first (P-84); B is where unboxed arithmetic happens; and D is the sizes in the model's own types (P-87). The whole preparation for the array work is to be done before the switch-over; only the work itself waits.

----
POSITIONS.md:113
- P-87 **The model's text is the notation, and the vocabulary is repaired around it.** The model is microGPT's two programs; the vocabulary is the array operations that they are written in (`FlatArrays.fss` for C4, the flat program, and `FlatArrays2.fss` for the APL-style one). No operator in the model is replaced by a function call to pass an overload check, as a proposed repair once wrote `planeSum(mask, x)` for `mask + x`; the vocabulary changes instead. Any repair that changes a line of the model is shown to the curator as a diff before it is built. Decision D, still open and returning after the switch-over with the other array decisions (P-85), is such a diff: it gives C4's arrays sized types, in its vocabulary's signatures and in the model lines that these force (`explorations/reviews/decision-d-diff.md`; the patch itself is only in git, in the parent of `84aef6a4f`). Nothing of decision D is applied before microGPT compiles, after the switch-over.

content.content:
- F-358 **In the scratch tree of F-352, a compiled loop over two `Array1` of 1,000 `RR64` against the one library ran about 45 times faster than under walk and of the order of 100 times slower than the same loop in Java; boxing explains 6 to 7 of that.** The loop is `s += a[i] b[i]`, 5 million iterations in the program's own `seq` loop: 1.4 s compiled as a process and 39.8 s under walk, about 0.8 s and 36 s without a one-line program's time. The Java loop over `double[]` takes 7.5 ms in a cold JVM and 4.4 ms warm. Each is one run; the Fortress and the Java ran in different sessions at different loads, the JIT's warm-up is inside the compiled 0.8 s, and the verifier was off. It is an order of magnitude and no more. Java models of the boxes put boxing at 6 to 7 times on a dot or matrix product (F-11). The rest has no measured share: the read through the store's wrapper with its checks and its `cast`, the range's closure for each iteration, and the transaction check and the box on the accumulator (F-12, row 641). It says nothing about microGPT's kernels: no matrix, no library reduction and no parallel loop ran. Detail: `compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/switch-rehearsal.md`, "5. One timing"; `reviews/plan-review-2026-11-10.md`, "7.3 What the first compiled timing says, and what it cannot say"; `java-baseline/REPORT.md`, "7. The rehearsal's loop".

- F-333 **The one library's arrays hold their elements in a Java-backed store in a field, which walk answers with its own `AtomicArray`.** `NativeArray` is a plain component: `PrimitiveArray` and `PrimImmutableArray` hold a `JavaArrayStore` of `FortressLibrary` in the field `mem` and read through `cast[\T\]`, `PrimImmutableRR64Array` a `JavaRR64ArrayStore`, now in the api with no factory choosing it (P-84, P-85). The stores' 7 bindings name `nativeHelpers/arrayOps` over the compiled `FortressArrayStore`, an `Object[]` whose elements the compiled transaction keys by array and index (`TXReadSlot`, `TXWriteSlot`), and `FortressRR64ArrayStore`, a `double[]`; NamingCzar's walk-world table reads the two classes as the two traits. Walk's loader answers each `arrayOps` name with `ArrayOps$<name>` over `FortressBuiltin`'s private `JavaArrayStoreObject`, an `AtomicArray`, and `JavaRR64ArrayStoreObject`, a `double[]`, and refuses a name with no operation at load. A second initialisation is ignored in both arrays, by walk's store and by `FortressArrayStore` (row 466); the two RR64 stores write it and answer `true`, as `PrimImmutableRR64Array`'s glue did. The stores' 7 bindings leave glue classes (F-299 holds the count). Tests: `tests/ArrayStoreWalk`, `ArrayStoreRR64Walk`, `ArrayInitOnceWalk`, `ArrayOpsMisspeltWalk`, `compiler/runtimeValues/ArrayStoreJUTest`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-array-store/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".

- F-385 **The class loader chooses a compiled call's opcode from the owner's class file, without loading the owner.** Where an instantiated template calls a method by `invokeinterface` on a type that becomes a plain class name, `MethodInstantiater.visitMethodInsn` reads `ACC_INTERFACE` from the class file that the loader would define for that name, and uses `invokevirtual` for a class (`runtimeSystem/MethodInstantiater.java`). So an object that lists a self-typed trait first, whose JVM superclass is that trait's default methods at the object, runs a default body that calls a method on a value of the self-type parameter (row 1052, fixed). Two limits, by reading, neither measured nor held by a test. The read keeps no cache, unlike the loader's lookup of generic expansions beside it, so each such call site of each expansion reads a class file. A class that the loader generates, such as a generic object's, has no class file, so the loader loads it as before, and a generic object that lists a self-typed trait first may still fail as row 1052 did. Test: `compiler_tests/SelfTypeParameterReceiverRun`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-self-arm-closure/REPORT.md`, "1. What changed and why", item 3; `reviews/batch-33-review.md`, "2. The decisions that landed at a default".

- F-264 **In the interpreter's library, nine `Vector` and `Matrix` operators and three branches of the array factories get their declared type through the function `cast`, and so does the sub-array that `Array2`'s column and row subscripts pass to `Col` and `Row`.** `cast[\T\](x)` returns `x` if it has type `T`, and raises `CastError` if not (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:33-37`). The operators are `Vector`'s `+`, binary and unary `-`, `scale` and `pmul`, and `Matrix`'s `+`, binary and unary `-` and `scale`. Each builds its result with the inherited `map` or `ivmap`, typed `Array1` or `Array2`, and so through `replica`, the method that makes an array of the same layout. The factory branches are those of `__builtinFactory1`, `__immutableFactory1` and `__builtinFactory2` for an array whose lowest indices are 0, each cast to its factory's declared result type. The subscripts are `a[:, j]` and `a[i, :]`. Each builds its sub-array with a range subscript, which answers an unsized `Array`, and the cast gives it the sized `Array2` that the field of `Col` or `Row` takes. Five bodies build with `fill` or `tabulate` and need no cast, since `Vector` and `Matrix` redeclare those two at their own type (F-158): the factories `vector(v)`, `tabulatedVector` and `matrix(v)`, and `Matrix`'s `rmul` and `lmul`. So the compiled checker accepts all these bodies (the distance stage). Under walk each cast holds at the eight number types (`tests/VectorMatrixCastsWalk.fss`). A `Vector` whose `replica` answers an array that is not a `Vector`, or a `Matrix` whose `replica` answers one that is not a `Matrix`, raises `CastError` at the nine operators. When the casts landed, no walk value moved in the 42 test files that use the array family, compared value by value, or in four array demos; every test of the interpreter's suite passed, and so did microGPT's quick pair. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-array-sites/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 5 (each change with its sites; walk's runs); `compile-ladder/rung-array-sites/SKEPTIC.md` sections 2 (the four demos) and 3, finding 3 (the `CastError` case).

- F-301 **On the compiled path a native helper is called through a generated wrapper over the box classes, and once the loop is hot C2 inlines the whole path, so the call costs nothing of its own.** A binding `builtinPrimitive("pkg.Class.method")` and a written `import java` alias call compile to the same bytes: an `invokestatic` of `native.pkg.Class.method`, a class the compiled path writes into `nativewrapper_cache/`, which unboxes each argument with `getValue`, calls the helper and boxes its result with `make`, a new box each time (`compiler/nativeInterface/FortressMethodAdapter.java:303-327`; `compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32.java:40-48`, where `make` now calls the `make` of the prelude's value object through a method handle, F-388). When the prelude declared its number types as traits, a functional method such as `ZZ32`'s `+` reached the wrapper through the dispatcher, an interface call, the springboard and the trait's static body. C2 inlines all of these frames, the helper, `make` and the box's constructor chain. Escape analysis then removes every temporary box, a helper's result passed into another helper among them, and one box stays per assignment to a mutable variable per iteration: 16 bytes for a `ZZ32`, 24 for an `RR64`. The library's form and the prelude's allocate the same. Observed once, while the prelude declared them as traits, and not since they are value objects, on one small program, `perf-probes/helper-calls/HelperCalls.fss`, by `javap`, C2's inlining log and the bytes that JFR counted, with no timing, on a machine shared at a load of 20 to 25; no test checks it. Detail: `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` sections 2 to 5.

- F-302 **In those loops C2 inlines down to depth 12 from the loop, against the 16 at which it stops by default, and a temporary box whose constructor chain passes the limit is no longer removed.** At JDK 25's default `MaxInlineLevel=15` a frame at depth d inlines when d is at most 16. When the prelude declared its number types as traits, their `+` reached `Object.<init>` under its result's box at depth 12, a top-level binding at 10. With the limit lowered to 8, a loop of two nested helper calls rose from 33 to 96 bytes per iteration, since its temporaries' chains no longer inlined. So an operator called from more than 4 further inlined frames keeps its temporary boxes. The chains measured are of that form, where the box extended its trait's springboard, and a springboard extends the springboard of its trait's first `extends` entry (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:5956-5963`). The prelude's box is now the class of its value object, over the payload class `FZZ32`, which extends `FValue` and no springboard (`compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32.java:22`; F-388), so its constructor chain no longer follows the type's `extends` entries. The depth of the value-object form is not measured. Observed once (F-301). Detail: `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` sections 3 and 4.

- F-106 **The native-wrapper generator wraps every method, static or instance, of a class that `import java` names, private ones too, but skips constructors, static initializers and every method with a Java `byte`, `short` or array type in its parameters or result. A wrapped method with a type that has no Fortress counterpart makes the generator refuse the whole import.** The generator writes the compiled path's Fortress wrappers for such a class. So a method of a `com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers` class that a library component names in `import java` needs a signature that maps to Fortress, private or not, unless the generator skips it. A class that no `import java` names is not bound by this: `systemHelper.setFinalStatic(Field, Object)` does not map. Gap-ledger row 368 records the refusal. Evidence: observed when a private helper with a `Class<?>` parameter broke the rebuild (`compile-ladder/rung-default-rendering/REPORT.md`, "The repair round"); the skips read in `FortressMethodAdapter.visitMethod` and `SignatureParser.unsayable`.

- F-183 **The compiled path's only array-like types are `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`, two hand-written Java classes declared only in its prelude and absent from the specification.** Each element access is boxed. No gated test makes or indexes a `ZZ32Vector` at run time. Gated tests make a `StringVector`, store two strings in it with `putValue` and assert its rendering (`compiler_tests/DefaultRenderRungS`), and read `args`, which is one (`Compiled2`). Passed to a generic object's constructor, either type fails at load: its descriptor class is `RTTIv`, where stamped code asks for `RTTIc`. Row 408 and `compiler_tests/XXXVecCtorLoad` hold this for a `ZZ32Vector`; the probe measured a `StringVector` too. A native helper cannot take a Java array, since the wrapper generator skips such methods. Detail: `compiler-probes/vectors/vectors.md` sections 1, 3 (step 9), 6 and 7.

- F-18 **On the compiled path, the class loader makes the class of a generic instantiation at its first use, by rewriting the template's bytecode with ASM, and the rewriting only renames, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field.** The class is `InstantiatingClassloader`; the `fortress-repo` skill's "The compiled runtime" gives the mechanism. A size is part of the made class's name, as in `pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, the object `Box` at size 3 in the probe component `pNatMeth`. Inside the class, the size's descriptor is `RTTIsize.of("<n>")` (F-129). A field of the template's type `T`, `LT;`, becomes `LFRR64;` in `Box⟦FRR64⟧`, and `[D` is no class name, so stamping alone keeps every number boxed (F-11). The team left two separate traces for unboxing. The plan in `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java` lists what to unbox: a primitive, a singleton object, unboxed fields, and a `comprises` clause whose types are unboxable; it says nothing of the loader or of instantiations. The loader has an empty "expando" stub (`runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`). A loader that stamps an `RR64` instance with a `double[]` field, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), does not exist and is unmeasured. Walk instantiates generics in its own evaluator, not by classes. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/java.md` section 1; `coordinator/array-design.md` section 2 (probe 1); `reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 3, way A4.

- F-350 **On the compiled path the arms of a parallel `do`, the elements of a tuple, the operands of an operator and the arguments of a call fork through one method, `CodeGen.genParallelExprs`, which joins every arm that it forked before an exception leaves the group; arguments fork where `ParallelismAnalyzer` marked the argument tuple.** The exception that leaves is that of the first arm, in the arms' order, that threw; when an exception leaves, an arm not yet forked is not run, and a `VirtualMachineError` leaves without the joins (`runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java:113-131`, `joinIfForked`). The analyzer marks no call written in the prelude's files, so the prelude's reductions run in sequence until the switch-over (row 982); the one library's parallel `ZZ32` range splits only a range of more than `grainSize`, 16, elements (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:20`, `:1320`, `:1337`). What it means: compiled against the one library, a reduction over more than 16 elements will fork its halves, and an exception leaves no arm running. By reading, not run: microGPT's vectors are 16, 16, 4 and 4 wide (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss:17`), so a reduction over one of them forks nothing on either path. Tests: `compiler_tests/AlsoArmThrowsJoinsCompiled`, `CallArgumentsForkCompiled`, `tests/ParRangeGrainWalk`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-forked-arguments/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "Points to report reached"; the model's widths against the grain: `reviews/batch-30-review.md`, "2. The three forks that landed at a default".

- F-139 **`RR32` is a sibling of `RR64` under `Number`, and `RR64` converts from it.** Nothing converts into `RR32`. Under `walk` two `RR32`s answer an `RR32`, and an `RR32` with an `RR64`, a float numeral or a `ZZ32` answers an `RR64`. A typed binding converts an `RR32`, but a declared return does not (row 387). On the compiled path `=` at the prelude's `RR32` overflows the stack (row 528), and two `RR32`s answer an `RR64` (row 529). Gated by `tests/RR32SiblingRungV.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-rr32-sibling/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 11.

- F-388 **The compiler's prelude declares its seven number types as value objects, whose classes the code generator writes over the run time's payload classes.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `RR32` and `RR64` are `value object`s in `CompilerBuiltin`; each object's class extends the abstract payload class `compiler/runtimeValues/F<T>`, which holds the JVM value. Descriptors, stamped instances and the RTTI's `className()` name the type by the payload class, while the RTTI's class stays the object's, so that the type lies below its traits at run time; a dotted call casts its receiver to the object's class; `F<T>.make` reaches the object's class's `make` by the name that `LibraryNames` gives, for the prelude only (the one library's seven have no rows yet, fork N4). So a program's object below a number type is refused at the compile, an overloading at `ZZ32` beside one at a program's trait is valid, a `typecase` clause at such a trait over a number is refused as unreachable (row 1081), and a number type named as a value does not compile (row 1082). Tests: `compiler_tests/NumberObjectsCompiled.test`, `compiler_tests/XXXNumberTypeExtendRefusedCompiled.test`, `compiler_tests/ComprisesMeetGenericTrait.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-number-payload-objects/REPORT.md`, "The design as built (a point to report)".

- F-352 **A compiled program has run against the interpreter's library only in a scratch tree with twelve marked hacks; on `main` the compile command reads the compiler's prelude unless `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` selects the one library (F-381).** In that tree, on `832f7d0d91`'s code, two lines of `Shell.useCompilerLibraries()` point the compiled path at the one library, and a one-line program then passes the checker and the code generator. Its run needs the library's fourteen components as bytecode, compiled by name in about 200 s. Three programs ran and printed walk's output: one that prints a line, one that builds and reads an `Array1`, and a dot product in the program's own loop over two `Array1`. Not run: an array of rank 2 or 3 (row 992, fixed since), the library's `DOT` and `SUM` (row 732, fixed since), and microGPT, which the checker stops (F-58). The runs met sixteen walls of two kinds. A test compiled against the prelude can show the first kind: the refusal of varargs (row 624), `label` (row 81), a closure class written twice (row 315), a method written twice (row 990), a missing cast at a `comprises` type (row 991), and rows 992 and 732; rows 81, 315, 990, 991, 732 and 992 are fixed since, and row 624 under the selection of the one library (F-390). Only a tree switched onto the one library shows the second kind: which run-time class carries each built-in type, a choice that reaches the code generator's naming (rows 874 and 995, row 995 now for the carried types other than the seven number types; row 866 is fixed; the one library's seven are not yet compiled over the payload classes, F-388); the trait table's search by the prelude's api names (row 942, fixed since; the search stays, and no compiled test reaches it, F-391); the dispatch method's package (row 994); `NN32`'s two getters (row 993). Every run had the JVM's verifier off, so the number of emitted methods that the verifier refuses is not known. Measured once; nothing of the scratch tree landed, and no test holds its runs. Detail: `compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/switch-rehearsal.md`, "2. The walls, in the order met", "4. How far each program got" and "6. The walls grouped, against PLAN's phase 4 and phase 5 lines"; `compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/model-closure-check.md`, "4. The checker's time for one program".

## 3. Question 2, decision A: what puts `double[]` under the library's generic array traits

**The question.** His decision of 2026-09-19 makes the store a JVM `double[]`, and the library's arrays are generic in their element type: `Vector[\T, nat s0\]` keeps its elements in `mem: PrimitiveArray[\T,s0\]` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2339-2345`). What makes a `Vector[\RR64, 16\]` hold a `double[]` while a `Vector[\T, 16\]` of another `T` keeps a boxed store?

**The mathematics.** None: the choice changes how the numbers are held, not what they mean.

**What each path does today.**

- Walk: every store is `PrimitiveArray`, boxed values in an `AtomicArray` (`coordinator/array-design.md` § 1). The team wrote one unboxed store: `object PrimImmutableRR64Array[\nat s0\]() extends ImmutableArray1[\RR64,0,s0\]` over a Java `double[]` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/NativeArray.fss:43-52`; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/PrimImmutableRR64Array.java`). Jan Maessen, 2008-07-28: "Immutable arrays of unboxed RR64. When you request an immutable array of RR64 these should be used in preference to the boxed version" (`353818213`). No library file names it; nothing selects it.
- The compiled path: stamping renames classes and cannot produce a `double[]` field (`coordinator/array-design.md` § 2, probe 1). The only unboxed stores are two hand-written Java classes, `FZZ32Vector` over an `int[]` and `FStringVector`, lowered straight to their classes by a table in the code generator; every element read is boxed through seven frames; a native helper cannot take a Java array (FACTS § The territory map, line 160).
- What an unboxed store buys alone, measured on 2026-09-20: nothing. The dot product over a `double[]` read and written through a boxing accessor is 8.9 times primitive, against 6.4 times for boxed storage; the matrix product 6.6 against 6.2 (`reviews/array-design-review.md`, Serious 4; `compiler-probes/array-design-review/java-medians.tsv`). The traffic is unboxed only by decision B, phase 6 (PLAN.md).
- The library's selection device, measured here on both paths (`reviews/array-design-ways/probes/`, one private cache per path; the compiled path in the compiler's own world, since the switch-over has not happened):
  - `WayANoCast.fss`: a generic factory with the library's witness `typecase` (`array1`'s, `FortressLibrary.fss:2375-2379`) whose `RR64` arm returns a store written for `RR64` alone. The checker refuses it, "Function body has type OR(DStore,BStore[\T\]), but declared return type is Arr[\T\]", as on 2026-09-20; walk runs it and picks `DStore` for `RR64`.
  - `WayACast.fss`: the same arm through the library's `cast`, `cast[\Arr[\T\]\](DStore(...))`, the device of `additiveIdentity` (`FortressLibrary.fss:3140-3155`). The checker accepts it. The compiled run and walk both print `RR64 DStore 1.5` and `ZZ32 BStore 7`.
  - `WayACastSized.fss`: the same with sizes, `vec[\T, nat n\]` returning `cast[\Vec[\T,n\]\](DVec[\n\](...))`. Accepted; both paths pick `DVec[\16\]` for `RR64` and the generic store for `ZZ32`, and a function with a shared size takes two of them.
  - `WayASpec.fss`: specialisation by overloading, a plain `mk(w: () -> RR64, x: RR64)` beside the generic `mk[\T\](w: () -> T, x: T)`, called from generic code with the library's witness. The checker accepts it and the compiled run dispatches to the plain declaration for `RR64` and to the generic one for `ZZ32`. Walk refuses the pair when it loads the program, "has a parameter with generic type, at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types", its declaration-time family check (rows 159 and 475).

**The specification.**

- "Fortress arrays are complex data structures; simple linear storage is encapsulated by the HeapSequence type, which is used in the implementation of arrays" (`Specification/advanced/parallelism-locality/arrays-distributed.tex:18-22`), marked not yet supported (`:15-16`).
- Jan Maessen's note on unboxed types, recorded in the draft: "Do we want to permit arrays of fixed bounds to be unboxed? No. Unboxed arrays are a different other thing. Among other things, an array of fixed bounds may be a segment of another array" (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:42`). The sized array is a structure; the linear store under it is what is unboxed.
- Jan's own example of the selection, in the draft's future work on overloading by static parameters: `array1[\T extends Object, nat s0\]()` beside `array1[\T extends Number, nat s0\](): Vector[\T,s0\]` (`future.tex:236-246`). The library's `array1` does it with the witness `typecase` meanwhile, "TODO: fix when Number is covariant" (`FortressLibrary.fss:2374`).
- The compiled encoding: "mentions of static parameters are replaced with their upper bounds" (`Papers/Implementation/MethodMapping.tex:134`), which is why stamping renames and nothing more.

**The commits.** David Chase's unboxing plan, "Cases for unboxing: 1) primitive. ZZ{8,16,32,64}, RR{32,64}, Boolean ... 3) unboxed fields" (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/optimization/Unbox.java:21-27`, first in `bce8b45ae`, 2009-03-07), referenced by nothing; and the loader's place for it, "if (false) { // Here will go all the magic expando-stuff." (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`, first in `4179cee84`, 2009-07-29).

**The peers.**

- .NET: "When a generic type is first constructed with a value type as a parameter, the runtime creates a specialized generic type ... Specialized generic types are created one time for each unique value type"; for reference types one shared version (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/generics/generics-in-the-run-time). A loader-made class per instantiation.
- Java: "JEP 218: Generics over Primitive Types", status Candidate: "extend generic types to support the specialization of generic classes and interfaces over primitive types" (https://openjdk.org/jeps/218).
- Scala: `@specialized` makes the compiler "generate specialized versions of generic code for specified types" (https://www.scala-lang.org/api/2.13.x/scala/specialized.html); Spire warns that "specialization will increase bytecode size by a factor of x2-10" (https://spire-math.org/guide.html).
- Haskell: `Data.Vector.Unboxed` "picks an efficient, specialised representation for every element type" through a data family chosen by the `Unbox` class (https://hackage-content.haskell.org/package/vector-0.13.2.0/docs/Data-Vector-Unboxed.html). A representation per element type, selected by the type.
- Julia, C++ and Rust compile a copy per concrete type (`reviews/size-runtime-design-brief.md` § 6).

**The ways.** Every way but A4 needs a hand-written Java store over `double[]`, on the `FZZ32Vector` pattern, and a Fortress object for it written for `RR64` alone, as `PrimImmutableRR64Array` is; they differ in what selects it.

1. **A1, the library's selection device with the library's `cast`** (`WayACast`, `WayACastSized`, measured). The generic factories `vector`, `matrix`, `array1` to `array3` and their tabulated forms test the witness and return the `RR64` store through `cast` for `RR64`, the generic store otherwise. The library's text keeps its generic types; the model's `vector[\RR64,s\]` gets the unboxed store with no line of its own. The cast is one run-time type test per array made, not per element (my reading). The draft's own spelling of the same selection is overloading by the element type's bound (`future.tex:236-246`); it still needs the cast to return a store written for one type (my reading).
2. **A2, specialisation by overloading on the witness** (`WayASpec`, measured). A plain factory for `RR64` beside the generic one; dispatch chooses from generic code. No cast. Walk refuses the pair at load today; answer 9's walk rung (batch 7b's W, "walk's choice by declared domains", PLAN.md) is where walk's family check changes, and whether it then takes this pair is not measured.
3. **A3, a factory name per element type,** `rr64Vector[\s0\]()` beside `vector[\T,s0\]()` (`reviews/array-design-review.md` § 3, decision A's A3). No selection at run time; the model names the `RR64` factory, and `vector[\RR64,s\]` stays boxed. The library's precedent is a factory name per kind of array: `array1`, `vector`, `primitiveArray`, `immutableArray` (`FortressLibrary.fsi:1428-1438`, `:1571-1579`).
4. **A4, the loader stamps a different class for an `RR64` instantiation,** the team's direction (`Unbox.java` cases 1 and 3, the loader's stub). `PrimitiveArray⟦FRR64,n⟧` gets a `double[]` field; no library line changes and nothing selects. The peers' shape (.NET, JEP 218, `@specialized` at compile time). The largest change, in the loader and the code generator; nothing of it exists and no probe has been run. An element read through the generic trait's `get` still returns a box unless decision B unboxes by static type (my reading).
5. **A5, a special type,** the compiled world's own precedent: an `RR64Vector` lowered to its Java class by the code generator's table, as `ZZ32Vector` is (FACTS line 160). A type the specification does not have; the model names it.

**What each costs.** A1: the store class and object, the bodies of the generic factories (`vector`, `matrix`, `array1` to `array3` and their value and function forms), a cast per array made; measured to check and run on both paths. A2: the same store, one plain factory per native element type, and walk's family check. A3: the store and one factory per element type; a model line wherever a factory is named. A4: loader and code-generator work of unknown size. A5: a type outside the specification. None changes the speed alone; decision B does (the measurement above).

## 6. Question 5: the element width, `RR32` or `RR64`

**The question.** microGPT's weights and activations are `RR64`. His premise (POSITIONS 2026-09-25, row 40's entry): language models are trained at 32-bit floats at most. Which width does the model use?

**The mathematics.** `RR32` is IEEE binary32: a 24-bit significand, about 7 decimal digits, unit roundoff 2^-24 ≈ 6e-8. `RR64` is binary64: 53 bits, about 16 digits, 2^-53 ≈ 1.1e-16. A sum of n terms can lose up to about n unit roundoffs; for the 4,192-term dot product that bound is about 2.5e-4 relative in `RR32` and 5e-13 in `RR64` (my reading of the standard bound).

**What each path does today.**

- The one library: `value object RR32 extends RR64` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:47`), a subtype, which the specification's "mutually exclusive" number types forbid. Its binary natives die when the other operand is any other number (row 435). A radix-point numeral at a typed `RR32` binding is refused on both paths, `a: RR32 = 1.5` (row 454), because a numeral with a radix point is a `FloatLiteral`, which extends `RR64` (`FortressBuiltin.fsi:44`). Batch 6.5b's rung V, in flight, makes `RR32` a sibling that `RR64` converts from, with its own arithmetic (`coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-6.5.md:219-227`).
- The compiler's prelude: `RR32` a sibling, `RR64` coercing from it (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:433-435`).
- C4 is `RR64` throughout: the type is named on 17 lines of `MicroGptFlat.fss`, 75 of `FlatArrays.fss` and 8 of `FlatData.fss`; 7 of the model's lines carry a radix-point numeral, among them `10.0^(-5)`, `0.0 MAX m0` and the `1.0 headDim` that turns a size into a float (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss:18`, `:29`, `:59`, `:60`, `:64`, `:66`, `:82`).
- The check: the goldens are the reference at "batch 1, float64" (`explorations/experiment/run-c-goldens/README.md:5`), and the tolerances are 1e-12 on losses and gradients and 1e-8 on finite differences (`run-c4/src/MicroGptFlatCheck.fss:16-18`), which only `RR64` can meet (my reading).
- The reference itself takes the width as an option: "dtype=fp32", `DT = np.float32 if args.get('dtype', 'fp64') == 'fp32' else np.float64` (`explorations/apl/reference/hsu-flat/microgpt_flat.py:12`, `:23`). So `RR32` goldens can come from the same unmodified script.
- On the JVM, measured here: the dot and matrix kernels of `perf-probes/kernels/java/` over `double[]` and over `float[]`, interleaved in one JVM, each kernel's pass timed 20 times a round (`reviews/array-design-ways/probes/width/WidthPair.java`). Two runs, each a pair in one JVM:
  - at a load of 9 (other runs), seven rounds (`WidthPair-1.txt`): the dot product 1.00 ms a pass in `double` and 1.02 ms in `float` (medians; ranges 0.94-1.17 and 0.96-1.41), the matrix product 0.55 and 0.44 ms (ranges 0.33-0.73 and 0.34-1.25);
  - at a load of 1.3, nine rounds (`WidthPair-2.txt`): the dot product 0.95 and 0.95 ms (ranges 0.81-0.99 and 0.94-0.97), the matrix product 0.56 and 0.59 ms (ranges 0.53-0.83 and 0.42-0.74).
  - The faster width changes between rounds and between runs, so neither run shows a difference beyond its noise. The `float` dot product's running sum ends at 231146.2 against 231145.27 in `double`, a relative difference of 4e-6.
- Memory: the parameter vector is 4,192 numbers, 33 KB as `double[]` and 17 KB as `float[]`.

**The specification.**

- `RR32` and `RR64` are "32 and 64-bit IEEE 754 floating-point numbers", and the draft's future work adds two functions on float types: `Double[\F\]`, "twice the size", and `Extended[\F\]`, "sufficiently larger than the floating-point type F to perform summations of reasonable size" (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:77-86`). That is mixed precision, in the draft's future work and never built.
- Type aliases, which would name the width once, are specified (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:631-650`), with the note that they are not yet supported (`:18`), and unimplemented (row 18); the 2012 restart comments the section out (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick:1008-1035`).

**The library's own practice.** `RR64` is the library's float: `Number.asFloat(self): RR64` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:284`), and the one unboxed store the team wrote is for `RR64` (`NativeArray.fss:43-52`). The witness `typecase`s list `RR32` as a leaf and make its values with `narrow(0.0)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3150`).

**The peers.** PyTorch: "When PyTorch is initialized its default floating point dtype is torch.float32" (https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.12/generated/torch.set_default_dtype.html). The reference defaults to float64 and offers float32 (above).

**The commits.** David Chase, 2009-08-31: "RR32 is NOT a subtype of RR64" (`6896886fb`, cited in `reviews/decisions-review/judgement.md` § 1).

**The ways.**

1. **5a, `RR64`, as written.** The goldens and tolerances stand, and the store is `double[]`, the words of his decision of 2026-09-19.
2. **5b, `RR32` throughout.** New goldens from the reference with `dtype=fp32`, tolerances restated at `RR32`'s scale. Every `RR64` in the model's and the vocabulary's types becomes `RR32`. Each radix-point numeral meets `RR32` through the library's explicit `narrow`, since a lossy conversion stays explicit (answer 8, POSITIONS 2026-09-26), unless the numeral types gain a conversion into `RR32`. The store is a `float[]` beside or in place of `double[]`, by question 2's mechanism. It waits for rung V.
3. **5c, the model generic in its width.** The model's functions take the element type as a static parameter. A numeral inside generic code becomes a `T` only through `x.one` or the witness `typecase` (FACTS line 61), so every constant of the model becomes a call (my reading; not measured).
4. **5d, the width named once by a type alias,** `type R = RR64`. One line switches the width. It needs type aliases built (row 18).
5. **5e, mixed: `RR32` storage with `RR64` accumulation,** the draft's `Extended[\F\]`. The library's reductions accumulate in the element's own type (`SUM` over `AdditiveGroup[\T\]`, FACTS line 116); the mixed products would be declarations such as a `DOT` of two `RR32` vectors answering `RR64`.

**What each costs.** 5a costs nothing now. 5b costs new goldens, every type line of the model and vocabulary, a narrowing at each float numeral, rung V, and a second store; it halves memory and changes the speed by the measured pair. 5c and 5d trade notation for a switch: 5c in every constant, 5d in a feature not yet built. 5e is new library declarations and a second store.

21:## 1. What an array is in the interpreter today
35:## 2. What the compiled world has
51:## 3. What microGPT needs from arrays
61:## 4. The options as they stood before the rulings
65:### (b) `double[]`-backed arrays with unboxed elements designed in
77:### (c) The library's generic traits over per-element-type native stores
89:## 5. What the specification and the team's own drafts say
103:## 6. The nat plan: what the second fork must deliver for the first
107:### 6a. What the checker and the code generator lack today
119:### 6b. What the team wrote, and what the interpreter does
127:### 6c. How the library's own nat declarations use them (92 lines in `FortressLibrary.fss`, 81 declarations; `NativeArray.fss` 3; `NatReflect.fss` 2)
145:### 6d. The compiled representation of a nat-sized `double[]` array
153:### 6e. The checker edit and the shadow route, assessed
161:## 7. The decision tree, with two questions closed
181:## 8. What happens right after the choice

71:What the code generator must learn, if the loops are to run unboxed in generated code: an element read must become `getfield val:[D`, `iload i`, `daload` instead of the four-call chain of §2, and a bare `double` must have somewhere to go, which means a local variable slot of descriptor `D` and `dadd`/`dmul` for `RR64` arithmetic whenever the checker's static type is `RR64`, boxing only where a value meets a `T` or an `Any`. That is unboxing by static type (`performance-roadmap.md` A1) in `CodeGen.java` (6,750 lines) and `VarCodeGen`; every rung of it is a `.java` rung under the full gate with the 85 files as the net. Without it, an unboxed store with boxed traffic is what `ZZ32Vector` is today; whether that alone is faster than boxed storage is not measured, and the Java model that would answer it is one more class in `perf-probes/kernels/java/`.
73:A second route to unboxed loops needs no code-generator change: write the loops of the vocabulary's operations as Java natives over `double[]` (the dot product, the matrix product, the elementwise maps, `SQRT`/`exp`/`log` over an array), so a box is paid once per whole-array operation instead of once per element. This is the shape of an APL implementation, each primitive a native loop, and microGPT in the C4 form is whole-array vocabulary; the residue is the user lambdas passed to `fill`, `map` and `rows`, which box per element. What the team shipped in this world is `ZZ32Vector`, and it is the only precedent with code behind it.

3:# The transaction checks: what the language requires, and the ways to remove them
5:## 1. A primer: what a transaction is in Fortress
36:- TxArray, a `while` loop over an array with mutable locals, 7 checks an element: 23.17 ns an element with the checks, 8.39 ns without, so 64 % of the time.
42:## 2. What the team's sources require
44:### 2.1 The specification
55:### 2.2 The team's later word
60:### 2.3 The team's two implementations
73:### 2.4 Who wrote it, and whether they planned to remove it

90:### 2.6 So: which variables can a transaction reach, by the specification?
107:## 3. The ways
111:- **TxArray** (64 %): `sumN` sums an eight-element vector, and `round` calls it 10 M times. All four of its `var`s, `acc`, `i`, `total` and `k`, are uncaptured locals in `while` loops:
152:### Way 1. The specification's shared and local objects (the team's own design, unbuilt)
161:### Way 2. A lexical rule for uncaptured locals, in the code generator
170:- **What it clears.** All 7 of TxArray's checks an element (the probe's 23.17 to 8.39 ns, since every check there is on an uncaptured local), and the library leaf's 6, or 4. None of TxScalar's or TxCell's, and not the store's.
175:**Way 2b, its second step: no cell for an uncaptured local.** The value lives in a JVM local slot. A block that writes it saves it in a second slot at its start, and restores it on an abort or an exception, before the retry or the rethrow: `atomic.tex:66`'s "any variable reverts". This removes the cell's allocation and `volatile` access, which the shadow kept, so 64 % is a lower bound here. An
177:### Way 3. Ask once per method call, not once per access
182:- **What it clears.** TxArray's 7 checks an element become about 1/8. TxScalar's and TxCell's 2 a step become 1, at the `apply` entry, so about half their share (inferred, not measured). It reaches captured locals, top-level `var`s and fields, but not the store.
186:### Way 4. Two versions of each method
189:- **Cost.** Code up to twice as large for the methods a block reaches. Three to five rungs (inferred). Outside `atomic` the JIT sees the original methods, so inlining improves as in Way 2.
196:### Way 5. One global switch: no checks until the first `atomic` runs
198:- **Changes.** Each check site becomes a guard that a block's first start turns off for good: in Java, a `SwitchPoint` behind an `invokedynamic` site. Generated code has no `invokedynamic` today (grep).
206:### Way 6. A whole-program analysis
214:### Way 7. A cheaper check (the run time only)
221:### Way 8. The specification's `io` and `atomic` modifiers
225:### Way 9. Change the language (listed as such)
235:## 4. How they weigh, and how they combine
237:- **For microGPT.** Way 2 clears the library leaf's 4 to 6 checks an element, where the kernels' variable checks are (by reading). Ways 3 to 6 also clear captured locals, which microGPT's model lines touch once a step. Only Ways 4 to 6 reach the store's per-element check (Way 3 with two store entry points), which is D1's ground as much as this one's.
238:- **By risk.** Way 2 is local to one method and rests on the specification's undo rule. Way 3 rests on an invariant of the run time (2.3). Ways 4 and 6 are large. Way 5's gain is lost by any program that opens a block.
239:- **By D2.** Way 2 (for uncaptured locals) and Way 7 stand under every answer. Ways 3, 4 and 5 are complete only under (a). Under (b) or (c) the question becomes "may another thread's transaction touch this?", and Way 1 or Way 6's second half carries it. Weak atomicity is what the peers ship: Deuce says so (Way 4), and X10, a peer the curator named (P-66), runs its blocks under one global lock
240:- **They combine.** Ways 2 and 2b go with every other way and take the uncaptured locals out first. Way 3 covers what Way 2 leaves. Way 4 makes Ways 3 and 5 unneeded. Way 7 helps whatever checks remain. Way 1 answers D2 beside any of them.
242:## 5. What needs measuring first, and when
244:- **Measured already, so not measured again.** Way 2's gain on TxArray is the probe's pair, 23.17 against 8.39 ns, since every check there is on an uncaptured local (`REPORT.md`, section 1). The shadow kept the bytecode, so removing the sites at compile time may gain more through inlining.

Also, the --warn-if-resolved=incubating option must be passed to the jmod tool, so that a warning is issued at compile time, link time, and run time if the incubator module is resolved.
